tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: PowerShell 7+ (pwsh)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` ARE available and work like bash. Prefer `cmd1 && cmd2` over `cmd1; cmd2` when cmd2 should only run if cmd1 succeeds.
   - Ternary (`$cond ? $a : $b`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are available.
   - Default file encoding is UTF-8 without BOM.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Write

Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file outside the working directory that you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

tools.name: SubagentHandback
tools.description:
Deliver your final report to the agent that spawned you (your caller). Use it once, for that hand-off only: when your work is complete, call SubagentHandback({message: <your full report>}) as your last tool call and then stop. It is not a messaging channel: do not use it for progress updates or questions.

Only a report delivered through SubagentHandback reaches your caller; plain text you write at the end of your turn is NOT delivered. There is no recipient parameter: the report can only go to your caller.

## remarkable
# reMarkable MCP Server

Access documents from your reMarkable tablet. All operations are read-only.

## Available Tools

- `remarkable_browse(path, query)` - Browse folders or search for documents
- `remarkable_read(document, content_type, page, grep)` - Read document content with pagination
- `remarkable_recent(limit)` - Get recently modified documents
- `remarkable_status()` - Check connection and diagnose issues
- `remarkable_image(document, page, include_ocr)` - Get a PNG image with optional OCR

## Recommended Workflows

### Finding and Reading Documents
1. Use `remarkable_browse(query="keyword")` to search by name
2. Use `remarkable_read("Document Name")` to get content
3. Use `remarkable_read("Document", page=2)` to continue reading long documents
4. Use `remarkable_read("Document", grep="pattern")` to search within a document

### Getting Page Images
Use `remarkable_image` when you need visual context:
- Hand-drawn diagrams, sketches, or UI mockups
- Content that text extraction might miss
- Implementing designs based on hand-drawn wireframes

Example: `remarkable_image("UI Mockup", page=1)` returns a PNG image
Example: `remarkable_image("Notes", include_ocr=True)` returns image with extracted text

### For Large Documents
Use pagination to avoid overwhelming context. The response includes:
- `page` / `total_pages` - current position
- `more` - true if more content exists
- `next_page` - page number to request next

### Combining Tools
- Browse → Read: Find documents first, then read them
- Recent → Read: Check what was recently modified, then read specific ones
- Read with grep: Search for specific content within large documents
- Browse → Image: Find a document then get its visual representation

## MCP Resources

Documents are registered as resources for direct access:
- `remarkable:///{path}.txt` - Get full extracted text content in one request
- `remarkableimg:///{path}.page-{N}.png` - Get PNG image of page N (notebooks only)
- Use resources when you need complete document content without pagination… [truncated]

Read-only access to the user's Zotero research library. For substantive sport-science questions, build a Zotero-first evidence pack before answering. Return bounded page-located evidence, label external fallback sources explicitly, and never represent a Reference Stub as a reviewed Paper Brief. SecondBrain Queue is the priority lane; promotion eligibility is controlled by promotion_scope.

11	**[00:00]** What is technique analysis? Technique analysis is a combination of biomechanics and kinesiology. Biomechanics is the study of human movement in the sports context. It's made up of mathematics, physics, Newtonian laws. Problem is it doesn't give us much in the way of practicality. As a coach, knowing that information is very important, but now what do I do with it? How do I apply it to my athletes to improve those numbers or decrease or increase those numbers, right? Whereas a technique analysis looks at the qualitative assessment of how the athletes move based off of their key force producing actions, the sequence of those actions, and knowing which muscles
12	
13	**[00:35]** are used, where they're used, how they're used. This now tells me more information and gives me more information from a practical standpoint of what we do. You know, profiling or technique analysis, whatever you wanna call it, is extremely important in my personal belief because if everything we're trying to do is get the athletes moving better on the field, well, let's assess it how they move. 16	
17	**[01:49]** but nothing too bad. And I remember it was yesterday, third game of the season, third quarter, he dropped back to pass and all of a sudden the ball went up and it looked like it got punted and you hear him screaming and he didn't get hit. He was by himself. He didn't hit an elbow, didn't hit the ground, nothing. His elbow fractured. He fractured [unclear elbow fracture term] and his throwing arm, just throwing a pass. Now, my boss at the time was an orthopedic surgeon. We were staying on the sideline. We got him into our practice and they x-rayed it and that's what it found. And he needed to get a screw in his arm. And our practice was gonna run his rehab.
18	
19	**[02:25]** So as he's going through the rehab, I knew that the mechanism of injury was one volume from doing too much, but also he didn't have great mechanics. Now, I did not have a background in biomechanics, so I didn't know what to do, but I knew that my mentor at the time, Mike Yosef Johnson was mentored by Dr. Michael Yessis, who was a PhD in biomechanics and brought over all the Russian research and studying that I've already been doing to the United States. So I asked Joseph, do you think Dr. Yessis would be interested in working with this boy based off of who his father was and me writing articles and publicizing it.
20	
21	**[03:02]** And he said, absolutely. So once the boy was able to start moving and doing a little more after the surgery and the screw was taken out of his elbow, we flew out to California and went to Doc's house. Now, Doc, we sent Doc some video of this boy throwing from the summer and everything before. So he had an idea of how his throwing mechanics and running and everything looked. And I'll never forget, as soon as we sat on his living room couch, Doc said, you have this wrong, this wrong, the sequence is off, and here's why I believe your elbow fractured. And so I was sold.
22	
23	**[03:39]** I was like, wow, that's pretty awesome. And then right away, 20 minutes later, we went out to a park and we started working on his running, his cutting, and his throwing mechanics with exercises, with special strength exercises, and then also some technical drills. And I was blown away. One at Doc's expertise in biomechanics, seeing it firsthand of assessing what happened. And then now the motor learning aspect of, now here's how we apply that. So that is what started me on this journey of technique analysis and wanting to know, okay, wow, if I'm trying to get my athletes better at moving, I should probably know
24	
25	**[04:15]** how movement occurs and how biomechanics and all this stuff works. And so that started my 15 year journey of apprenticing under Dr. Michael Yesses. And again, I wanted to put this course together for many reasons, but also partly is a little bit of a love letter to Dr. Yessis because of how much he meant to me and how much he contributed to our industry and the work that he did.

112	**[00:39:29]** Bernstein wrote that an improvement of a motor skills consist of establishing the pathway of achieving the needed goal, the motor pattern, which is resistant to its possible fluctuations under the influence of environmental conditions. This establishing of a motor pattern occurs through the assimilation of the essential parameters of a motor task, motor determinants with gradual adaptation to its non-essential parameters to the environmental conditions. So there's the quote from the book. And I brought this up in the last module, right? For the solution of the motor problems, the organism must distinguish between essential variables and non-essential variables. That's what he talked about. These are quotes from Bernstein. Essential variables are key factors the motor system consciously controls
113	
114	**[00:40:15]** or prioritizes to achieve a specific motor goal. Non-essential variables refer to factors or components not vital to the core functionality. The organism tries to realize the essential variables by completely overcoming any difficulties and influences from the environment. As for the parameters of non-essential variables, the organism, on the contrary, is yielding adaptively. In short, the organism is active towards the form and reactive towards the latter. So they're active towards the essential variables and they're reactive to the non-essential variables. Now, little do people know that Yuri Verkhoshansky was a student of Nikolai Bernstein and has actually met him and had in past letters were Bernstein.
115	
116	**[00:41:01]** Right. And. Verkhoshansky came up with this idea of key movements that in every motor skill, there are two fundamental components. There's key movements which are critical for managing motor tasks and producing the resulting power output and secondary movements assisting the key movements during the complete competition exercise execution. It means that to increase the power output of a given competition exercise, it is necessary to increase the working effect of its key movements. Two, to improve the efficiency of the interaction between the key movements and between the key movements and the secondary movements. Right. So that is how we improve the power output in the competition exercise.
117

# How to Watch Film

**What it is** — The practical method for ecologically-informed performance analysis.

**Live analysis is not enough.** The complexity of the problems, and of the solutions organised against them, makes real-time assessment next to impossible if you want an accurate reading. Analysis happens on video.

**Watch widely.** Myszka's practice with a new NFL player is to watch **every single snap the player has taken in the league** (via NFL+ or NFL Rewind), then, depending on age and status, college film — even highlights — and sometimes high school. The rationale: you cannot determine where a player should go without unpacking how their movement skill came to be. Trends across a career are visible through the context-content lens that are invisible in a season.

**Watch each play from as many vantage points as possible** — sideline, endzone, all-22 — and **at various speeds** — full, half, super slow motion. Cross-checking across conditions is what keeps a detail from being an artefact of one angle.

**Two honesty rules the chapter insists on:**

1. **Nonlinearity is real.** A player highly attuned one day can be overwhelmed by similar problems the next, for any number of reasons. Minor changes in the problem can produce dramatic changes in the solution, and vice versa.
2. **Absence of evidence is not evidence.** No two problems are the same and some problems the player has simply never faced. **Do not fret if you finish an analysis without enough to make a proclamation, good or bad.** Saying "I have not seen this player solve that problem" is a legitimate finding — and it is often the most actionable one, because it names an exposure gap ([[case-study--tight-end-punt-coverage-exposure-gap]]).

**Why it works** — Breadth substitutes for the experiment you cannot run. You cannot present a player with a controlled problem set, so you find the range of problems they have already met.

**When to apply** — Any serious individual analysis. The volume prescription is the part most people skip and the part that produces the trend.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**: this is one practitioner's method, offered without validation, and the authors concede it "can all sound quite daunting and may seem like overkill." Watching every career snap is not feasible for most staff at most levels, and there is no guidance here on what a reduced version preserves. Access also constrains it — what film you can get depends on your role. Treat the *principles* (multiple angles, multiple speeds, breadth over depth, comfort with an inconclusive verdict) as the transferable part.

**Example** — A staff with two hours per player should spend them on twelve plays from three angles rather than one play frame by frame. The trend is the finding; the frame is the illustration.
======

# Functional Variability

**What it is** — Variability in human movement is **inherently present** in neurobiological systems (Button et al., 2020; Chow et al., 2016), and it is **beneficial** for solving dynamic problems — which rejects the traditional project of teaching idealised patterns (Chow et al., 2006). Everyone is different and capable of solutions uniquely their own, so coaches should **inject variability into practice to encourage exploratory behaviour** — through purposeful constraint manipulation, or by encouraging athletes to search for different ways of solving the problem.

The word doing the work is **functional**. Variability is assessed by **how practical and useful the solution was in solving the problem** — not by how different it was.

**Why it works** — The chapter's worked example is unusually concrete. A group of defensive backs explore their coverage strategies — backpedal, shuffle (the 50/50 technique), angle breaks, zone and speed turns — against receivers running the routes and tactical situations they will actually see. Following Orth et al. (2017) on creative solutions emerging from exploration, the exploration happens at two levels:

- **The coordination strategy itself** — using a shuffle instead of the backpedal they are accustomed to; using a zone turn where they would normally be instructed to use a speed turn, such as when a receiver attacks their blind spot.
- **The control parameters within a solution** — centre-of-mass height, base-of-support width, speed into the break, length of the penultimate step before planting, amount of body lean, the specific angle of the break.

That second list is the practical gift. It is a menu of things a player can vary *without* changing what they are doing, which makes variability available even inside a tightly constrained situation.

**When to apply** — Any time you want exploration but cannot change the activity — a rehab window, an install period, a positional drill you do not control. The control parameters can be varied within almost anything.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**: the rejection of idealised patterns is well-argued and the underlying variability literature is solid, but the specific coaching prescription here is illustrative rather than trialled. And **functional is the constraint, not an afterthought** — variation that does not get tested against a real problem is just noise, and a player who explores without feedback from an actual outcome learns nothing about fit. In rehabilitation, the control-parameter list also needs filtering: centre-of-mass height and penultimate step length are exactly the parameters a clinician may be deliberately restricting.

**Example** — A defensive back in a limited return-to-play window cannot yet run every route concept. He can still vary base width, lean, and speed into the break against a single receiver — and find out which combinations actually cover.
=====

# Individualization

**What it is** — Training must be matched to the individual athlete's abilities, potential, learning characteristics, and the demands of their sport — at every performance level. Copying a successful athlete's or elite program wholesale onto a different (especially younger) athlete is the central error this principle guards against. The plan is built from a comprehensive read of the athlete's work capacity.

**Why it works** — Adaptation depends on the individual's capacity to absorb load. That capacity is set by training history, health status, life stress, and chronological/biological/training age (see [[heuristic--biological-vs-training-age]]). Crucially, **stressors are additive**: school, work, family, travel, and training sum together, so the same session is not the same dose for two athletes — or for one athlete in two different weeks.

**When to apply** — Prescribing load for a mixed-readiness group; deciding when to deviate from a template; reducing load during high external-stress periods (e.g., exam weeks); explaining why a junior shouldn't run an elite's program.

**When NOT to apply** — Full individualization isn't always necessary or feasible — athletes at a similar development stage can share much of a plan, so reserve detailed individualization for where capacities genuinely diverge. It also requires real monitoring data; without periodic testing it degrades into guesswork.

**Example** — During exam week a collegiate athlete's accumulated academic stress is treated as part of total load, so the S&C dose is trimmed even though the training-only prescription would have stayed the same.

# How to Watch Film

**What it is** — The practical method for ecologically-informed performance analysis.

**Live analysis is not enough.** The complexity of the problems, and of the solutions organised against them, makes real-time assessment next to impossible if you want an accurate reading. Analysis happens on video.

**Watch widely.** Myszka's practice with a new NFL player is to watch **every single snap the player has taken in the league** (via NFL+ or NFL Rewind), then, depending on age and status, college film — even highlights — and sometimes high school. The rationale: you cannot determine where a player should go without unpacking how their movement skill came to be. Trends across a career are visible through the context-content lens that are invisible in a season.

**Watch each play from as many vantage points as possible** — sideline, endzone, all-22 — and **at various speeds** — full, half, super slow motion. Cross-checking across conditions is what keeps a detail from being an artefact of one angle.

**Two honesty rules the chapter insists on:**

1. **Nonlinearity is real.** A player highly attuned one day can be overwhelmed by similar problems the next, for any number of reasons. Minor changes in the problem can produce dramatic changes in the solution, and vice versa.
2. **Absence of evidence is not evidence.** No two problems are the same and some problems the player has simply never faced. **Do not fret if you finish an analysis without enough to make a proclamation, good or bad.** Saying "I have not seen this player solve that problem" is a legitimate finding — and it is often the most actionable one, because it names an exposure gap ([[case-study--tight-end-punt-coverage-exposure-gap]]).

**Why it works** — Breadth substitutes for the experiment you cannot run. You cannot present a player with a controlled problem set, so you find the range of problems they have already met.

**When to apply** — Any serious individual analysis. The volume prescription is the part most people skip and the part that produces the trend.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**: this is one practitioner's method, offered without validation, and the authors concede it "can all sound quite daunting and may seem like overkill." Watching every career snap is not feasible for most staff at most levels, and there is no guidance here on what a reduced version preserves. Access also constrains it — what film you can get depends on your role. Treat the *principles* (multiple angles, multiple speeds, breadth over depth, comfort with an inconclusive verdict) as the transferable part.

**Example** — A staff with two hours per player should spend them on twelve plays from three angles rather than one play frame by frame. The trend is the finding; the frame is the illustration.
======

# Functional Variability

**What it is** — Variability in human movement is **inherently present** in neurobiological systems (Button et al., 2020; Chow et al., 2016), and it is **beneficial** for solving dynamic problems — which rejects the traditional project of teaching idealised patterns (Chow et al., 2006). Everyone is different and capable of solutions uniquely their own, so coaches should **inject variability into practice to encourage exploratory behaviour** — through purposeful constraint manipulation, or by encouraging athletes to search for different ways of solving the problem.

The word doing the work is **functional**. Variability is assessed by **how practical and useful the solution was in solving the problem** — not by how different it was.

**Why it works** — The chapter's worked example is unusually concrete. A group of defensive backs explore their coverage strategies — backpedal, shuffle (the 50/50 technique), angle breaks, zone and speed turns — against receivers running the routes and tactical situations they will actually see. Following Orth et al. (2017) on creative solutions emerging from exploration, the exploration happens at two levels:

- **The coordination strategy itself** — using a shuffle instead of the backpedal they are accustomed to; using a zone turn where they would normally be instructed to use a speed turn, such as when a receiver attacks their blind spot.
- **The control parameters within a solution** — centre-of-mass height, base-of-support width, speed into the break, length of the penultimate step before planting, amount of body lean, the specific angle of the break.

That second list is the practical gift. It is a menu of things a player can vary *without* changing what they are doing, which makes variability available even inside a tightly constrained situation.

**When to apply** — Any time you want exploration but cannot change the activity — a rehab window, an install period, a positional drill you do not control. The control parameters can be varied within almost anything.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**: the rejection of idealised patterns is well-argued and the underlying variability literature is solid, but the specific coaching prescription here is illustrative rather than trialled. And **functional is the constraint, not an afterthought** — variation that does not get tested against a real problem is just noise, and a player who explores without feedback from an actual outcome learns nothing about fit. In rehabilitation, the control-parameter list also needs filtering: centre-of-mass height and penultimate step length are exactly the parameters a clinician may be deliberately restricting.

**Example** — A defensive back in a limited return-to-play window cannot yet run every route concept. He can still vary base width, lean, and speed into the break against a single receiver — and find out which combinations actually cover.
=====

# Individualization

**What it is** — Training must be matched to the individual athlete's abilities, potential, learning characteristics, and the demands of their sport — at every performance level. Copying a successful athlete's or elite program wholesale onto a different (especially younger) athlete is the central error this principle guards against. The plan is built from a comprehensive read of the athlete's work capacity.

**Why it works** — Adaptation depends on the individual's capacity to absorb load. That capacity is set by training history, health status, life stress, and chronological/biological/training age (see [[heuristic--biological-vs-training-age]]). Crucially, **stressors are additive**: school, work, family, travel, and training sum together, so the same session is not the same dose for two athletes — or for one athlete in two different weeks.

**When to apply** — Prescribing load for a mixed-readiness group; deciding when to deviate from a template; reducing load during high external-stress periods (e.g., exam weeks); explaining why a junior shouldn't run an elite's program.

**When NOT to apply** — Full individualization isn't always necessary or feasible — athletes at a similar development stage can share much of a plan, so reserve detailed individualization for where capacities genuinely diverge. It also requires real monitoring data; without periodic testing it degrades into guesswork.

**Example** — During exam week a collegiate athlete's accumulated academic stress is treated as part of total load, so the S&C dose is trimmed even though the training-only prescription would have stayed the same.

_book.md

# Prescriptive Coaching Narrows a Player's Solution Set

**What it is** — Telling athletes the one correct technique measurably reduces the number of movement solutions they can produce, and the creativity of what they do in competition.

- **Lee et al. (2014), youth tennis forehand, six weeks.** Prescriptive group: "move the racquet low to high by turning the shoulders to the side and contacting the ball in front of the forward foot." Analogy group: **"hit the ball like the shape of a rainbow."** Principal components analysis clustered players by how they actually moved. Both groups began with **four** solution clusters. After training, the prescriptive group had **three**; the analogy group had **eight**.
- **Santos et al. (2018), soccer, five months.** Prescriptive training versus differential learning (constant random variation in surface, field shape, ball type — never the same action twice in a row). Creativity was rated in real matches, before and after, by two blinded raters using the Creative Behavior Assessment in Team Sports. The prescriptive group's actions were rated **significantly less versatile, original and creative.**
- **Orangi et al. (2021b), soccer, 12 weeks.** A prescriptive group instructed in ideal shooting, passing and dribbling technique produced **three times fewer creative actions** in a test match than a CLA group that received no technical instruction and practised in small-sided games with varied player numbers, area and rules.

# The Sprint Coaching Eye: Local Actions and Global Views

**What it is** — Moyer's two-level way of watching a sprinter. The **local view** is three "key force-producing actions": (1) **knee drive** — the thigh driven forward from behind the body right after toe-off; (2) **pawback** (swing-leg retraction) — the leg driven back and down into the ground; (3) **ankle joint extension** — plantar flexion through push-off. # Faster Sprinters Swing the Thigh Faster ("Whip From the Hip")

**What it is** — Moyer cites Ken Clark's work to support his "switching" observation: across subjects and trials in Clark's "whip from the hip" study, **thigh angular velocity showed a strong positive linear correlation with running speed** and with lower-limb vertical velocity at touchdown. He adds Clark's later work on **horizontal foot speed** (the foot moving backward relative to the body before contact, sometimes called negative foot speed, measured with shoe-mounted inertial sensors) and Peter Weyand's summary that the fastest sprinters "cock the knee high before driving the foot into the ground while maintaining a stiff ankle". His own addition, made in the live session: **"you can't whip if the thigh doesn't go high"** — pawback speed depends on how high knee drive took the thigh first.

**Why it works** — Asserted mechanism: a faster swing brings the foot down and back at higher speed, so the foot lands closer under the centre of mass (less braking) and the lower limb strikes the ground harder, which supports the large, brief vertical forces fast running needs (Clark and Weyand's two-mass model). The research relationship is **correlational and cross-sectional** — faster runners swing faster. It does not show that training thigh speed makes an athlete faster. Moyer also says, lovingly, that Clark "regurgitates" what 1980s Soviet reports already found; that is his opinion about priority, not a finding.

**When to apply** — As the evidence base for watching switching on film; as a reason to include hip-flexor and swing-speed work in a speed block; when reading GPS max velocity next to film (an athlete whose top speed stalls often shows a low thigh in front and slow retraction).

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**, not higher: the citations were read aloud on slides and were not checked against the papers in this ingest. Correlation across a speed range partly reflects the fact that running faster *requires* a faster limb swing — it is close to a description of speed rather than a separate cause of it. Do not coach "paw back" as a cue in isolation: the live session records the common failure where athletes cast the foot out in front and pull it back, which lands the foot ahead of the hips. Moyer says he teaches pawback only when needed, and always with the foot landing as close under the body as possible.

**Example** — Two receivers top out at 9.1 m/s on GPS. On side film one shows a high thigh and fast retraction; the other's thigh barely passes horizontal and the foot drops straight down. The second athlete is the candidate for knee-drive and retraction work, and his next GPS top speed is the check.

**Related** — [[claim--hip-flexor-fatigue-degrades-sprint-mechanics]] — the same thigh action is what Moyer says fails first under fatigue.

# The Ankle Plantar Flexors as the Main "Driving Link" at Top Speed

**What it is** — Moyer's case that the foot and ankle, not the knee, drive the push-off at maximal speed. He strings together figures from several sources:
- Soleus and gastrocnemius generate **77% of vertical and 60% of horizontal** centre-of-mass acceleration; the soleus gives vertical support at all speeds, the gastrocnemius more horizontal propulsion.
- The Achilles tendon "accumulates **75–90%** of the mechanical energy" (source not named).
- From a 1981 *Soviet Sports Review* article out of Zatsiorsky's lab: during takeoff external energy rises by **340 J**; knee muscles do **31 J**, plantar flexors **192 J** ("more than six times as much"), so "the main driving link in running with maximum sustained speed is the foot". The foot-ankle returns **60–70%** of the landing energy.
- Push-off "can generate up to **20%** of the force" in sprinting (attributed to Yessis; Moyer says in the live session he does not know where that figure came from).

**Why it works** — Asserted mechanism: the foot and ankle work eccentrically then concentrically in each contact, storing energy in the tendon as the body passes over the foot and giving it back at push-off. The training conclusion he draws is to develop the "spring-like properties of the foot, calves and tendons" — calf strength, ankle plyometrics, foot work.

**When to apply** — As a reason to keep calf, Achilles and foot work in a speed programme (single-leg calf raises, ankle-dominant plyometrics, isometrics), and to look at the ankle when an athlete sinks at contact.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **untested**: these are force- and energy-share figures quoted from slides, mixing different measures (muscle contribution to acceleration, tendon energy storage, joint work) from different studies and different speeds, none checked in this ingest. They cannot be added together, and "20% of the force" sits awkwardly next to "192 of 340 J". The 77%/60% figure resembles musculoskeletal-modelling results (e.g. Dorn, Schache and Pandy's running simulations), which are model outputs, not measurements. Joint-work studies of maximal sprinting generally find the **hip** dominates at the highest speeds, with the ankle's share plateauing — so "the foot is the main driver" should not be repeated as settled. The practical advice (train the calf-Achilles complex) does not depend on these numbers being right.

**Example** — A running back's contact looks soft on film and his ankle collapses. Moyer's framework says train the calf-Achilles spring; a sound version of that is to add single-leg calf strength and ankle hops and re-film, without citing "the Achilles does 90% of the work" to the athlete.

**Related** — [[framework--sprint-coaching-eye-local-and-global-views]] — ankle extension is the third local key action. The knee-extension-at-toe-off argument that Moyer builds on these figures (knee should not exceed ~165°) is covered in a separate, contested entry.

# Hip-Flexor Fatigue as the Limiter of Sprint Mechanics

**What it is** — Moyer cites two *Soviet Sports Review* reports. The 1981 article (Zatsiorsky's lab, "biomechanics of the takeoff in running") concluded that the hip-joint flexors are among the most energy-consuming muscles of the stride, that their fatigue "makes the biomechanical conditions of the takeoff worse" — less amortisation in the distal joints, less pre-stretch — and that "major attention should be given to developing local speed endurance of the hip joint muscles, mainly the flexors". The 1989 article on fatigue-induced changes in sprint technique found "the limiting factor in running speed is the fatigue of the hip joint flexors", showing up as **lower thigh height, less pawback and longer support (ground contact) phases**. He shows a recent repeated-sprint study in football athletes with a similar pattern, and links the fatigued pattern — anterior pelvic tilt, leaning forward, backside-dominant stride — to hamstring risk.

**Why it works** — Asserted mechanism: if the thigh does not rise, there is less range to whip it back, the foot lands later and further forward, and the athlete spends longer on the ground, which spoils the elastic contact. # Faster Sprinters Swing the Thigh Faster ("Whip From the Hip")

**What it is** — Moyer cites Ken Clark's work to support his "switching" observation: across subjects and trials in Clark's "whip from the hip" study, **thigh angular velocity showed a strong positive linear correlation with running speed** and with lower-limb vertical velocity at touchdown. He adds Clark's later work on **horizontal foot speed** (the foot moving backward relative to the body before contact, sometimes called negative foot speed, measured with shoe-mounted inertial sensors) and Peter Weyand's summary that the fastest sprinters "cock the knee high before driving the foot into the ground while maintaining a stiff ankle". His own addition, made in the live session: **"you can't whip if the thigh doesn't go high"** — pawback speed depends on how high knee drive took the thigh first.

**Why it works** — Asserted mechanism: a faster swing brings the foot down and back at higher speed, so the foot lands closer under the centre of mass (less braking) and the lower limb strikes the ground harder, which supports the large, brief vertical forces fast running needs (Clark and Weyand's two-mass model). The research relationship is **correlational and cross-sectional** — faster runners swing faster. It does not show that training thigh speed makes an athlete faster. Moyer also says, lovingly, that Clark "regurgitates" what 1980s Soviet reports already found; that is his opinion about priority, not a finding.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**, not higher: the citations were read aloud on slides and were not checked against the papers in this ingest. Correlation across a speed range partly reflects the fact that running faster *requires* a faster limb swing — it is close to a description of speed rather than a separate cause of it. Do not coach "paw back" as a cue in isolation: the live session records the common failure where athletes cast the foot out in front and pull it back, which lands the foot ahead of the hips. Moyer says he teaches pawback only when needed, and always with the foot landing as close under the body as possible.

**Example** — Two receivers top out at 9.1 m/s on GPS. On side film one shows a high thigh and fast retraction; the other's thigh barely passes horizontal and the foot drops straight down. The second athlete is the candidate for knee-drive and retraction work, and his next GPS top speed is the check.

# The Ankle Plantar Flexors as the Main "Driving Link" at Top Speed

**What it is** — Moyer's case that the foot and ankle, not the knee, drive the push-off at maximal speed. He strings together figures from several sources:
- Soleus and gastrocnemius generate **77% of vertical and 60% of horizontal** centre-of-mass acceleration; the soleus gives vertical support at all speeds, the gastrocnemius more horizontal propulsion.
- The Achilles tendon "accumulates **75–90%** of the mechanical energy" (source not named).
- From a 1981 *Soviet Sports Review* article out of Zatsiorsky's lab: during takeoff external energy rises by **340 J**; knee muscles do **31 J**, plantar flexors **192 J** ("more than six times as much"), so "the main driving link in running with maximum sustained speed is the foot". The foot-ankle returns **60–70%** of the landing energy.
- Push-off "can generate up to **20%** of the force" in sprinting (attributed to Yessis; Moyer says in the live session he does not know where that figure came from).

**Why it works** — Asserted mechanism: the foot and ankle work eccentrically then concentrically in each contact, storing energy in the tendon as the body passes over the foot and giving it back at push-off. The training conclusion he draws is to develop the "spring-like properties of the foot, calves and tendons" — calf strength, ankle plyometrics, foot work.

**When to apply** — As a reason to keep calf, Achilles and foot work in a speed programme (single-leg calf raises, ankle-dominant plyometrics, isometrics), and to look at the ankle when an athlete sinks at contact.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **untested**: these are force- and energy-share figures quoted from slides, mixing different measures (muscle contribution to acceleration, tendon energy storage, joint work) from different studies and different speeds, none checked in this ingest. They cannot be added together, and "20% of the force" sits awkwardly next to "192 of 340 J". The 77%/60% figure resembles musculoskeletal-modelling results (e.g. Dorn, Schache and Pandy's running simulations), which are model outputs, not measurements. Joint-work studies of maximal sprinting generally find the **hip** dominates at the highest speeds, with the ankle's share plateauing — so "the foot is the main driver" should not be repeated as settled. The practical advice (train the calf-Achilles complex) does not depend on these numbers being right.

**Example** — A running back's contact looks soft on film and his ankle collapses. Moyer's framework says train the calf-Achilles spring; a sound version of that is to add single-leg calf strength and ankle hops and re-film, without citing "the Achilles does 90% of the work" to the athlete.

**Related** — [[framework--sprint-coaching-eye-local-and-global-views]] — ankle extension is the third local key action. The knee-extension-at-toe-off argument that Moyer builds on these figures (knee should not exceed ~165°) is covered in a separate, contested entry.

# Assess the Action That Produced the Position, Not the Silhouette

**What it is** — Moyer's first rule of assessment, borrowed from a Randy Huntington line: people talk about **positions**, but what matters is **the actions used to reach them**. Do not hold an athlete up against a still frame of Bolt, Michael Johnson or Tyreek Hill and coach the difference; those shapes come from anthropometrics and physical qualities your athlete does not have. Instead ask which of the key actions (knee drive, pawback, ankle extension) is under-performing, and train that. He pairs it with two companion ideas: **know what is inefficient before you know what is ideal** ("there is no ideal, but there is an efficient"), and separate **effective** from **efficient** — an athlete can be fast while running in a way that costs them tissue over a season.

**Why it works** — A position in a still frame is the end result of forces applied earlier in the stride. Coaching the shape ("get your knee up", "stay tall") asks the athlete to copy an outcome without changing what produced it, so the shape either does not appear or appears as a posed imitation. Changing the capacity or timing of the action that produces the position is what changes the position. That logic is sound; the claim that his three key actions are the right levers is his selection.

**When to apply** — Any time a staff member is about to cue a posture off a photo; when a player arrives with a "fix your arm angle" note from a camp; when an athlete is fast but keeps getting soft-tissue injuries (effective but perhaps not efficient). In football, where body types range from 170-lb corners to 320-lb linemen, the rule stops elite-sprinter imitation.

**When NOT to apply** — Some positions *are* worth coaching directly — a start stance, a first-step shin angle — because they are set before the action and are the athlete's choice. The effective/efficient split is also his framing: "the cost of running like that over time" is a hypothesis about injury, not a measured cost, so do not rebuild a fast, healthy athlete's stride because it looks inefficient. And "coach the action" still depends on correctly identifying which action is at fault, which is an unvalidated visual judgement.

**Example** — A linebacker's front-side thigh never rises above about 60° in the photo. Rather than cueing "knee up", staff check hip-flexor strength and hip-extension range, add knee-drive and wicket work, and re-film in four weeks to see whether the thigh rises on its own.

**Related** — [[claim--prescriptive-coaching-narrows-adaptability]] — agreement: both reject coaching to a model shape. Tension: Moyer still believes in a set of correct key actions.

# Moyer's Sprint Fault Checklist by View and Phase

**What it is** — The things Moyer actually looks for on film, collected from lessons 6, 14 and 15. He starts every look with **foot contact** — his "number one" item.

*Foot contact (every view)*
- Which part of the foot lands — forefoot, midfoot, whole foot, heel — and **where relative to the hips and the knee**. Heel strike landing ahead of the knee is his biggest red flag.
- Space **between the knees at contact**: "zero to a little". A gap means slow switching (knee drive and/or pawback).

*Side view, upright running*
- Toe-off: slight knee bend (a fully straight knee he reads as an ankle/calf limitation — this reading is disputed).
- Swing leg folding: heel should come close to the buttock. A **long lever** (shin hanging open) means knee drive is poor and the shin whips out early.
- The opposite fault: **excessive heel recovery** behind the body (from behind you cannot see the buttocks because the foot is so high) — a big backside sweep with poor front side.
- Thigh height in front and whether the foot comes **back and down** into the ground or just drops straight down.
- Sinking at contact: how much hip, knee and ankle flexion; do they "mush"? Bounce of a ponytail is a quick read of vertical oscillation.

*Early acceleration*
- Landing slightly ahead of the hips is acceptable; how far ahead is the question. A step landing far in front ("power walking") with a **vertical shin at contact** is a fault.
- **Thigh spread at toe-off** (projection). Little spread = a "Fred Flintstone" frequency runner.
- How early they **stand up** — upright within ~5 yd means poor projection / horizontal force.

*Front and rear views (start from the ground up)*
- Does the foot roll to and **push through the big toe** with a straight foot? Some rotation is fine; the degree matters.
- Ankles collapsing inward; external rotation at toe-off.
- **Pelvic drop** / side-to-side "sloshing" at stance — a stiffness fault.
- **Crossover gait** — feet landing on or across the midline.
- From the front the swing-leg foot should be **hidden behind the thigh**; seeing it means a long lever.

**Why it works** — Each item maps to one local action or global quality ([[framework--sprint-coaching-eye-local-and-global-views]]), so a fault on film points to a training category rather than a cue. That is the value: it turns watching into a decision.

**When to apply** — Building a film-review template for speed testing; a shared sheet so athletic performance and athletic medicine staff describe the same thing the same way; RTP running sessions filmed side-on and from the front.

**When NOT to apply** — This is **Moyer's personal checklist, not a validated screen**: no reliability data, no thresholds (how much knee gap, how much pelvic drop), and several items rest on his untested injury beliefs (heel strike, long lever). The "straight knee at toe-off means an ankle problem" item is disputed elsewhere in the course. Use it to describe and track, not to diagnose or clear an athlete. Several items (pelvic drop, rotation, crossover) need a true front or rear camera, not a phone at an angle.

**Example** — Summer testing: each player's flying 10 is filmed side-on at 240 fps plus one front view. A graduate assistant ticks the checklist per athlete; athletes with three or more flags go to a follow-up range-of-motion check ([[heuristic--match-sprint-fault-to-rom-check-before-intervening]]).

# Film Several Sprints, From Several Angles, and Note the Conditions

**What it is** — Moyer's filming habits, stated in passing rather than as a protocol. He never judges an athlete on **one sprint from one view**; he wants a set of sprints from different angles (side-on for the stride, front and rear for foot, ankle and pelvis). He **records the conditions** that could distort the picture — his first film of a pro football player was on a **wet track in flat basketball shoes**, so he told himself to "take it with a grain of salt". He notes the **intent** of the run: timed sprints, where the athlete is chasing a number, can look different from drill work. He watches live first for the global picture, then breaks the film down (Dartfish or a phone) for the key actions. In the live session he adds that from the front or back he always reads **from the ground up**.

**Why it works** — A single rep mixes the athlete's pattern with noise from surface, footwear, fatigue, effort and camera angle. Several reps from more than one view let you see what repeats — the pattern — and discard what does not.

**When to apply** — Any baseline sprint film; before an RTP progression step; before deciding a player "has" a fault. Write down surface, footwear (cleats vs trainers), temperature, the rep's place in the session, and whether it was timed.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **supported**: it is sensible practice, but the course gives no protocol — no frame rate, camera height, distance, or number of reps. Build those yourself and keep them fixed, or before/after comparisons are not comparable. Watching live for "global" impressions is quick but unreliable at full speed; do not act on live impressions alone.

**Example** — A receiver's first film shows a heel-first contact, but he was in turf shoes on a wet field. Re-filmed in cleats on dry turf across four reps, contact is midfoot on three of four. The "fault" was mostly the conditions.

**Related** — [[heuristic--how-to-watch-film]] — agreement: multiple angles, multiple speeds, comfort with an inconclusive verdict.

# Assess the Action That Produced the Position, Not the Silhouette

**What it is** — Moyer's first rule of assessment, borrowed from a Randy Huntington line: people talk about **positions**, but what matters is **the actions used to reach them**. Do not hold an athlete up against a still frame of Bolt, Michael Johnson or Tyreek Hill and coach the difference; those shapes come from anthropometrics and physical qualities your athlete does not have. Instead ask which of the key actions (knee drive, pawback, ankle extension) is under-performing, and train that. He pairs it with two companion ideas: **know what is inefficient before you know what is ideal** ("there is no ideal, but there is an efficient"), and separate **effective** from **efficient** — an athlete can be fast while running in a way that costs them tissue over a season.

**Why it works** — A position in a still frame is the end result of forces applied earlier in the stride. Coaching the shape ("get your knee up", "stay tall") asks the athlete to copy an outcome without changing what produced it, so the shape either does not appear or appears as a posed imitation. Changing the capacity or timing of the action that produces the position is what changes the position. That logic is sound; the claim that his three key actions are the right levers is his selection.

**When to apply** — Any time a staff member is about to cue a posture off a photo; when a player arrives with a "fix your arm angle" note from a camp; when an athlete is fast but keeps getting soft-tissue injuries (effective but perhaps not efficient). In football, where body types range from 170-lb corners to 320-lb linemen, the rule stops elite-sprinter imitation.

**When NOT to apply** — Some positions *are* worth coaching directly — a start stance, a first-step shin angle — because they are set before the action and are the athlete's choice. The effective/efficient split is also his framing: "the cost of running like that over time" is a hypothesis about injury, not a measured cost, so do not rebuild a fast, healthy athlete's stride because it looks inefficient. And "coach the action" still depends on correctly identifying which action is at fault, which is an unvalidated visual judgement.

**Example** — A linebacker's front-side thigh never rises above about 60° in the photo. Rather than cueing "knee up", staff check hip-flexor strength and hip-extension range, add knee-drive and wicket work, and re-film in four weeks to see whether the thigh rises on its own.

**Related** — [[claim--prescriptive-coaching-narrows-adaptability]] — agreement: both reject coaching to a model shape. Tension: Moyer still believes in a set of correct key actions.

# Moyer's Sprint Fault Checklist by View and Phase

**What it is** — The things Moyer actually looks for on film, collected from lessons 6, 14 and 15. He starts every look with **foot contact** — his "number one" item.

*Foot contact (every view)*
- Which part of the foot lands — forefoot, midfoot, whole foot, heel — and **where relative to the hips and the knee**. Heel strike landing ahead of the knee is his biggest red flag.
- Space **between the knees at contact**: "zero to a little". A gap means slow switching (knee drive and/or pawback).

*Side view, upright running*
- Toe-off: slight knee bend (a fully straight knee he reads as an ankle/calf limitation — this reading is disputed).
- Swing leg folding: heel should come close to the buttock. A **long lever** (shin hanging open) means knee drive is poor and the shin whips out early.
- The opposite fault: **excessive heel recovery** behind the body (from behind you cannot see the buttocks because the foot is so high) — a big backside sweep with poor front side.
- Thigh height in front and whether the foot comes **back and down** into the ground or just drops straight down.
- Sinking at contact: how much hip, knee and ankle flexion; do they "mush"? Bounce of a ponytail is a quick read of vertical oscillation.

*Early acceleration*
- Landing slightly ahead of the hips is acceptable; how far ahead is the question. A step landing far in front ("power walking") with a **vertical shin at contact** is a fault.
- **Thigh spread at toe-off** (projection). Little spread = a "Fred Flintstone" frequency runner.
- How early they **stand up** — upright within ~5 yd means poor projection / horizontal force.

*Front and rear views (start from the ground up)*
- Does the foot roll to and **push through the big toe** with a straight foot? Some rotation is fine; the degree matters.
- Ankles collapsing inward; external rotation at toe-off.
- **Pelvic drop** / side-to-side "sloshing" at stance — a stiffness fault.
- **Crossover gait** — feet landing on or across the midline.
- From the front the swing-leg foot should be **hidden behind the thigh**; seeing it means a long lever.

**Why it works** — Each item maps to one local action or global quality ([[framework--sprint-coaching-eye-local-and-global-views]]), so a fault on film points to a training category rather than a cue. That is the value: it turns watching into a decision.

**When to apply** — Building a film-review template for speed testing; a shared sheet so athletic performance and athletic medicine staff describe the same thing the same way; RTP running sessions filmed side-on and from the front.

**When NOT to apply** — This is **Moyer's personal checklist, not a validated screen**: no reliability data, no thresholds (how much knee gap, how much pelvic drop), and several items rest on his untested injury beliefs (heel strike, long lever). The "straight knee at toe-off means an ankle problem" item is disputed elsewhere in the course. Use it to describe and track, not to diagnose or clear an athlete. Several items (pelvic drop, rotation, crossover) need a true front or rear camera, not a phone at an angle.

**Example** — Summer testing: each player's flying 10 is filmed side-on at 240 fps plus one front view. A graduate assistant ticks the checklist per athlete; athletes with three or more flags go to a follow-up range-of-motion check ([[heuristic--match-sprint-fault-to-rom-check-before-intervening]]).

# "Every Athlete With Non-Contact Running Pain Was a Heel Striker"

**What it is** — Moyer's strongest personal claim: in years of assessment he has "never assessed an athlete who had any non-contact related pains that was not a heel striker" — patellar tendon, Achilles, shin splints, hamstring. He calls heel striking "an epidemic with youth athletes" and the first thing he looks for and corrects. His picture: a heel striker lands ahead of the centre of mass and often ahead of the knee, which he likens to driving home with the emergency brake on. Athletes moved to a mid- or forefoot contact report feeling "bouncy" or "springy", which he takes as a sign they are now using the elastic return.

**Why it works** — Asserted mechanism: landing ahead of the body increases braking force and time under load, sends force "to places we don't want", and lengthens contact. The braking part is plausible for **overstriding** (foot far ahead of the centre of mass), which is not the same thing as **which part of the foot lands first**; Moyer treats the two as one.

**When to apply** — As a reason to look at foot contact first on any running film, and to include contact position in an RTP running assessment for patellar tendon, calf-Achilles and hamstring cases. Moving an athlete's contact closer under the hips is a low-risk target.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **untested**. "Never seen one who wasn't" comes from a clinic that sees injured runners, with no count of uninjured heel strikers, no blinding, and a coach who looks for heel striking first — every kind of selection and confirmation bias is present. In team sport, where most athletes rarely reach full upright speed and many heel-strike at jogging speeds, heel contact is very common among uninjured players. The distance-running literature has not shown that changing foot strike reduces injury, and changing it shifts load to the calf and Achilles. Do not tell an injured athlete their heel strike caused the injury.

**Example** — A tight end with patellar tendon pain lands heel-first well ahead of the knee at 80% speed. The defensible target is reducing overstride (landing closer under the hips) while monitoring calf-Achilles load, not "never land on your heel".

**Related** — [[claim--long-swing-lever-and-heel-strike-hamstring-hypothesis]] — his hamstring-specific version of the same idea.

# In Return to Run, Watch Them Run

**What it is** — Moyer's complaint from years in an orthopaedic practice: rehab clinics treat a running injury (patellar pain, a hamstring strain) with generic exercises — TKEs, knee extensions, Nordics, bridges, isometrics, then a short-to-long running programme — **without ever watching the athlete run**. The pain goes, the athlete "goes back to running like crap", and the injury returns. His process instead: (1) gather **injury history, training background and current goals**; (2) know the **sport's demands**; (3) **watch and film them run** before choosing interventions; (4) **re-film after** the rehab block to see whether mechanics or left-right differences actually changed. He states that "gym strength is less important than how they apply force to the ground during running", so a running-specific test is essential for judging progress.

**Why it works** — Clinical tests and gym strength measure capacities; sprinting is the task that injures. If the running pattern that loaded the tissue is unchanged, capacity gains may not protect it. Filming before and after gives a direct check that the task has changed, not just the tests. The logic is sound; his framing that "research indicates biomechanical analysis can predict injuries" overstates the evidence, which is mostly associations.

**When to apply** — Every lower-limb soft-tissue RTP at Baylor: film the athlete's running at each progression stage (tempo, 75%, 90%, max), side and front, and compare with pre-injury film when it exists. Pair film with GPS max velocity and force-plate or NordBord asymmetry so the decision has both a task view and a capacity view. Moyer quotes that about a third of hamstring injuries recur, with the highest risk in the first two weeks back — the window where running film is most useful.

**When NOT to apply** — Film shows *how* they run, not tissue readiness; it does not replace strength, range, imaging or clinical criteria, and "runs well" is not a clearance test. Changing mechanics during late rehab also adds a new stressor at a vulnerable time — record mechanics, but be careful about making big technique changes in the final days before clearance. His injury statistics (25–35% of team-sport injuries are hamstrings, "some show 50%") were quoted loosely.

**Example** — A cornerback cleared on NordBord symmetry and pain-free isometrics is filmed at 90%. Side view shows his injured leg still swinging a long lever and landing further ahead than the other. Staff hold the progression one stage and add swing-leg work before max-velocity exposure.

**Related** — [[claim--long-swing-lever-and-heel-strike-hamstring-hypothesis]]; [[principle--action-capacity-is-not-skill]] — agreement: capacity scores do not show how the task is performed.

# Four Acceleration Profiles (After J. J. Wild) as a Starting Point for Training

**What it is** — Moyer uses J. J. Wild's research (introduced to him by Jonas Dodoo's Speedworks group) that sorts team-sport athletes' early-acceleration strategies into four groups from step length, step rate, contact time and flight time. His labels and descriptions:
1. **Bounders — step length + air-based.** Long strides and good projection, but they pop up vertically; hips rise too early.
2. **Drivers — step length + ground-based.** Long strides and good projection, but very little air time; hips stay low with no rise; "mushy", not bouncy.
3. **Spinners — step frequency + ground-based.** Quick steps that "spin the wheels"; the foot barely leaves the ground.
4. **Bouncers — step frequency + air-based.** Quick steps but bouncing up and down; looks like jumping. He also calls this the "Fred Flintstone" runner (he uses that label loosely elsewhere).

His training response is to **move each athlete toward the middle**, not into a best quadrant: bounders a little more ground-based (more force into the ground, especially in acceleration); drivers a little more bouncy; spinners better projection plus a bit more bounce; bouncers better projection and more force. Live-session examples: for **bounders**, ankle range work, heavy sleds, single-leg calf raises, pawback work (banded marches, banded bounding); for **drivers**, foot isometrics, squats with a pause, pawbacks, and extensive jumps for stiffness.

**Why it works** — Categorising reduces complexity (he quotes Stu McMillan): in a squad of 20–40, four buckets let you individualise the first 10–15 minutes of a session with four or five group-specific exercises while the rest of the plan stays common.

**When to apply** — Group individualisation in team speed sessions; a first-pass sort after camp testing, using side-on film of the first 10 yd (plus timing gates or GPS acceleration data if available).

**When NOT to apply** — Wild's categories come from measured kinematics; Moyer's use is a **qualitative, by-eye sort**, with no reliability data and no reported evidence that bucket-specific training beats common training. The four labels (bounders etc.) may be Moyer's or Speedworks' shorthand rather than Wild's — check before citing. His training response per bucket is his own opinion; responses for spinners and bouncers were stated only in outline. A profile is a strategy, not a fault — strong defensive linemen may be "drivers" for good reasons over 5 yd. Do not use the bucket to predict injury (see [[claim--acceleration-profile-predicts-injury-site]]).

**Example** — Of 16 skill players, four are bounders. In the first 12 minutes of speed day they do heavy sled marches and single-leg calf raises while the drivers do pogo series and pawback drills; everyone then runs the common acceleration session.

**Related** — [[principle--individualization]] (periodization--bompa) — agreement: individualise where capacities genuinely diverge; buckets are a cheap middle ground.

# Acceleration Profile Linked to Injury Site

**What it is** — As Moyer reports it, J. J. Wild also looked for injury patterns across the four acceleration profiles (one study shown was in female team-sport athletes) and found them:
- **Quadrant 1 (bounders — length, air):** calf, Achilles and foot.
- **Quadrant 2 (drivers — length, ground):** patella and quad; hip and thigh.
- **Quadrant 3 (spinners — frequency, ground):** hip flexors and adductors.
- **Quadrant 4 (bouncers — frequency, air):** calf, Achilles, foot and hip flexors — the widest spread of soft-tissue injuries.

He summarises that "sprint acceleration strategies can be linked to specific injury sites", with examples such as poor hamstring engagement in acceleration causing hamstring strains and excessive braking in the first steps straining the calf.

**Why it works** — Asserted: each strategy loads different tissues more heavily (e.g. more braking in the first steps loads the calf). That is plausible but not demonstrated here.

**When to apply** — As a prompt for what to watch in an athlete who already fits a profile — for example, extra attention to calf-Achilles load monitoring in athletes who pop up early.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **untested**. The figures were shown on slides and not described (sample, design, effect sizes, whether the injuries came before or after the profiling are all unknown). Injury-site associations from small observational samples are unstable. Moyer's own bucket assignments are made by eye. His causal examples ("poor hamstring engagement causes hamstring strains") are stated as fact without support. Do not screen or restrict athletes by profile, and read the original Wild work before citing any of this.

**Example** — A bouncer-profile wideout reports calf tightness. The profile is a reason to look closer at his calf load and contact mechanics — not evidence that his profile caused it.

**Related** — [[framework--wild-four-sprint-acceleration-profiles]].

# "Every Athlete With Non-Contact Running Pain Was a Heel Striker"

**What it is** — Moyer's strongest personal claim: in years of assessment he has "never assessed an athlete who had any non-contact related pains that was not a heel striker" — patellar tendon, Achilles, shin splints, hamstring. He calls heel striking "an epidemic with youth athletes" and the first thing he looks for and corrects. His picture: a heel striker lands ahead of the centre of mass and often ahead of the knee, which he likens to driving home with the emergency brake on. Athletes moved to a mid- or forefoot contact report feeling "bouncy" or "springy", which he takes as a sign they are now using the elastic return.

**Why it works** — Asserted mechanism: landing ahead of the body increases braking force and time under load, sends force "to places we don't want", and lengthens contact. The braking part is plausible for **overstriding** (foot far ahead of the centre of mass), which is not the same thing as **which part of the foot lands first**; Moyer treats the two as one.

**When to apply** — As a reason to look at foot contact first on any running film, and to include contact position in an RTP running assessment for patellar tendon, calf-Achilles and hamstring cases. Moving an athlete's contact closer under the hips is a low-risk target.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **untested**. "Never seen one who wasn't" comes from a clinic that sees injured runners, with no count of uninjured heel strikers, no blinding, and a coach who looks for heel striking first — every kind of selection and confirmation bias is present. In team sport, where most athletes rarely reach full upright speed and many heel-strike at jogging speeds, heel contact is very common among uninjured players. The distance-running literature has not shown that changing foot strike reduces injury, and changing it shifts load to the calf and Achilles. Do not tell an injured athlete their heel strike caused the injury.

**Example** — A tight end with patellar tendon pain lands heel-first well ahead of the knee at 80% speed. The defensible target is reducing overstride (landing closer under the hips) while monitoring calf-Achilles load, not "never land on your heel".

**Related** — [[claim--long-swing-lever-and-heel-strike-hamstring-hypothesis]] — his hamstring-specific version of the same idea.

# In Return to Run, Watch Them Run

**What it is** — Moyer's complaint from years in an orthopaedic practice: rehab clinics treat a running injury (patellar pain, a hamstring strain) with generic exercises — TKEs, knee extensions, Nordics, bridges, isometrics, then a short-to-long running programme — **without ever watching the athlete run**. His process instead: (1) gather **injury history, training background and current goals**; (2) know the **sport's demands**; (3) **watch and film them run** before choosing interventions; (4) **re-film after** the rehab block to see whether mechanics or left-right differences actually changed. He states that "gym strength is less important than how they apply force to the ground during running", so a running-specific test is essential for judging progress.

**Why it works** — Clinical tests and gym strength measure capacities; sprinting is the task that injures. If the running pattern that loaded the tissue is unchanged, capacity gains may not protect it. Filming before and after gives a direct check that the task has changed, not just the tests.
