# Acceleration Profile Linked to Injury Site

**What it is** — As Moyer reports it, J. J. Wild also looked for injury patterns across the four acceleration profiles (one study shown was in female team-sport athletes) and found them:
- **Quadrant 1 (bounders — length, air):** calf, Achilles and foot.
- **Quadrant 2 (drivers — length, ground):** patella and quad; hip and thigh.
- **Quadrant 3 (spinners — frequency, ground):** hip flexors and adductors.
- **Quadrant 4 (bouncers — frequency, air):** calf, Achilles, foot and hip flexors — the widest spread of soft-tissue injuries.

He summarises that "sprint acceleration strategies can be linked to specific injury sites", with examples such as poor hamstring engagement in acceleration causing hamstring strains and excessive braking in the first steps straining the calf.

**Why it works** — Asserted: each strategy loads different tissues more heavily (e.g. more braking in the first steps loads the calf). That is plausible but not demonstrated here.

**When to apply** — As a prompt for what to watch in an athlete who already fits a profile — for example, extra attention to calf-Achilles load monitoring in athletes who pop up early.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **untested**. The figures were shown on slides and not described (sample, design, effect sizes, whether the injuries came before or after the profiling are all unknown). Injury-site associations from small observational samples are unstable. Moyer's own bucket assignments are made by eye. His causal examples ("poor hamstring engagement causes hamstring strains") are stated as fact without support. Do not screen or restrict athletes by profile, and read the original Wild work before citing any of this.

**Example** — A bouncer-profile wideout reports calf tightness. The profile is a reason to look closer at his calf load and contact mechanics — not evidence that his profile caused it.

**Related** — [[framework--wild-four-sprint-acceleration-profiles]].

# Show a Sprint Change as Matched Video Plus a Performance Number, and Let Your Eye Set the Plan

**What it is** — Moyer's standard for claiming a result: the industry "talks about results but doesn't show video evidence". He shows **before-and-after video of the same sprint** side by side, and where he has it a **performance measure** (10-yd and 20-yd splits). He uses AI motion software (he names ViewMotion, "Binary", Altus, Ken Clark's app, and SpeedWorks' projection-switching-reactivity scores) and likes it — but for **education and selling**: showing parents, coaches and athletes a change they could not see in raw video. His rule: **"it doesn't change my decision at all."** The intervention comes from what he sees in the key actions, not from the score.

**Why it works** — Video shows *what* changed; a time or speed shows whether it *mattered*. Either alone is weak: better-looking mechanics with no faster time may be cosmetic, and a faster time with no film cannot say why. Keeping the software as communication rather than the decision-maker protects against a score measuring something other than what you think (see [[heuristic--low-sprint-reactivity-score-check-foot-placement]]).

**When to apply** — Reporting speed-development work to head coaches or position coaches; RTP updates; any time a block of technical work needs to justify its time. At Baylor: matched side-on film at testing plus timing-gate splits or GPS max velocity from practice.

**When NOT to apply** — "Comparable video" needs to be genuinely comparable — same camera position, surface, footwear, effort and time of session — or the before-and-after mostly shows filming differences. A single pre and post time is within normal day-to-day variation for many athletes (hand-timed or single-trial gate times especially). Moyer's own examples do not separate his technical work from strength training, growth or simply being coached for six weeks, so they illustrate the reporting format, not proof that the method works. Also note he sells coaching and uses these clips to market it.

**Example** — Pre-camp and post-camp, each skill player runs two flying 10s through gates, filmed from the same spot at 10 yd. The report shows the best time each day next to paired stills at toe-off and touchdown — with a note if the conditions differed.

**Related** — [[case-study--six-week-sprint-before-after-cases]].

# A Low Reactivity Score May Be Foot Placement, Not a Stiffness Deficit

**What it is** — Moyer's caution about AI sprint software: a **low reactivity (stiffness) score** is often read as "this athlete is not stiff or bouncy enough", which points to plyometrics and stiffness work. He argues that for many of his athletes the real cause is **where the foot lands** — poor pawback / swing-leg retraction puts the foot too far in front, the athlete spends longer on the ground, and that long contact "presents itself as" low stiffness. The score is right that contact is long; it is wrong about why.

**Why it works** — Asserted: contact time and vertical movement, which such scores are likely built from, depend on both the spring qualities of the leg and on touchdown position. A foot that lands far ahead has to be passed over before push-off, lengthening contact even in a stiff leg. So the same number can have two causes that need different training. The mechanism is reasonable; the claim that it is the cause "with some of these athletes" is his observation.

**When to apply** — Any time a derived score (reactivity, stiffness, RSI from a sprint, contact-time flags from a wearable) drives a training decision. Before prescribing stiffness work, look at side-on film at touchdown: where is the foot relative to the hips? If it is far ahead, work retraction and contact position first and see whether the score moves.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **untested**: no data were shown for how often this happens, and the internal formula of the software he refers to (SpeedWorks' reactivity score) was not described. An athlete can have both problems. And the reverse error is possible — calling everything a foot-placement problem when the athlete genuinely sinks at contact.

**Example** — A receiver's reactivity score is the lowest in his group. Side film shows his foot landing well ahead of his hips with a fairly firm ankle and knee. Staff spend three weeks on pawback and wicket work instead of adding depth jumps, and the score rises with no change in jump testing.

**Related** — [[principle--pair-sprint-change-with-video-and-a-time]].

# Three Short-Block Sprint Cases: HS Football, College WR, HS Sprinter

**What it is** — Three of Moyer's "results" cases from lesson 11, each shown as before/after video.
1. **High-school football player, ~6 weeks.** Diagnosis by eye: poor projection ("a spinner, Fred Flintstone kind of runner", tall and lanky) and poor stiffness ("mushes"). Work: lots of ankle- and calf-focused plyometrics, many single-leg calf raises, and heavy sled work. Shown with ViewMotion and SpeedWorks projection/switching/reactivity scores; projection clearly improved, stiffness scores "not great" still. No times given.
2. **College football wide receiver, ~6 weeks.** 10-yd split **1.25 → 1.15 s**; the second figure **1.73 → 1.63 s**. Interventions not described.
3. **High-school sprinter.** Only calf work and swing-leg retraction work — "we didn't change much as far as heavy sleds or squatting". After, she lands attacking back and down instead of dropping straight down. No times given.

**Why it works** — Moyer's reading: fixing the specific key action he identified (projection and stiffness in case 1; retraction in case 3) produced the visible change. That is his interpretation.

**When to apply** — As worked examples of matching a diagnosis to a narrow training emphasis, and of the reporting format (video plus a time).

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **untested**. No control, one athlete per case, and several changes at once in case 1 (plyos, calf work, heavy sleds) — plus growth in high-school athletes and simply having six weeks of coaching. The WR times have an **internal inconsistency**: Moyer calls 1.73 "the second 10", but a second 10-yd split slower than the first from a standing start is not plausible; 1.73 is more likely the 20-yd time. If so, the total gain is 0.10 s, not the "two tenths" he states. Single-trial times of this size are within normal variation for hand or single-gate timing, and the timing method was not given. Treat these as illustrations, not evidence.

**Example** — Case 3 is the cleanest template for Baylor use: one diagnosed action (retraction), one narrow training emphasis, and a visible, filmable change in touchdown position — the kind of case worth reproducing with gate times attached.

**Related** — [[principle--pair-sprint-change-with-video-and-a-time]]; [[case-study--sprint-swing-lever-angle-66-to-45]].

# Measuring a Long Swing Lever: 66.6° to 45° in a Pro Athlete

**What it is** — A professional athlete (context across lessons 6, 7 and the live sessions suggests an NFL player with a hamstring history, though the lessons do not confirm it is the same person) had a switching problem: the swing leg did not fold, creating a **long lever**, and he had a long history of soft-tissue treatment on his hip flexors. Moyer froze a side-on frame in **Dartfish** and measured the swing-leg angle at **66.6°**. After **one to two months** ("a month later, two months later") of **pails and rails** (FRC-style isometric range work), **Lila wearable resistance** and **wicket runs**, the same measure was **45°** on the stop frame — "we took off 21 degrees". He claims this is faster, more effective, and less wear on the hip flexors and rectus femoris.

**Why it works** — Asserted: a shorter lever is easier and faster to swing forward, so the thigh can come through without the hip flexors and rectus femoris having to drive a long, heavy pendulum. That follows from basic moment-of-inertia physics; that it improved his speed or reduced his injury risk was not measured.

**When to apply** — The useful part is the **method**: turn a by-eye fault into a number with a single frame from comparable side-on video. At Baylor this is a cheap way to track fold-up side to side in an athlete with a hamstring history, or across an RTP.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **untested**. Moyer did not define the angle (most likely the knee angle between thigh and shank at a point in swing — a smaller angle means more fold), nor which frame, nor camera set-up; a single frame at a slightly different moment of swing can change such an angle by many degrees. No speed data were reported. Three interventions ran together, and Moyer coaches with and markets wearable resistance (Lila), so the attribution to it is conflicted. Before using this measure yourself, fix the frame rule (e.g. the frame where the swing-leg thigh passes the stance leg), camera height and distance, and average across several strides and both legs.

**Example** — A cornerback returning from a left hamstring strain: at the frame where the swing thigh passes the stance leg, left knee angle 70°, right 52°. Re-measured every two weeks through RTP alongside NordBord asymmetry, it gives a running-specific number to go with the strength one.

**Related** — [[claim--long-swing-lever-and-heel-strike-hamstring-hypothesis]].

# Technique Analysis: The Sequence of Key Force-Producing Actions and the Muscles Doing Them

**What it is** — Moyer's (and his mentor Michael Yessis's) definition. **Biomechanics** is the physics of movement — numbers, forces, Newton's laws — and on its own "doesn't give us much in the way of practicality": a coach who knows an angle or a force still has to decide what to do. **Technique analysis** combines biomechanics with kinesiology into a **qualitative assessment of three things**: (1) the **key force-producing actions**, (2) the **sequence** in which they happen, and (3) **which muscles do them, where in the range, and how**. The muscle part is what makes it actionable — it names the exercise to train.

**Why it works** — Knowing the sequence and the working muscles lets the analyst go straight from "what is wrong" to "what to train", which a number alone does not do. Moyer's origin story makes the principle concrete: as a high-school strength coach in 2010, he saw his starting quarterback's elbow fracture while throwing a pass with no contact, after a summer of heavy throwing volume. When they sent the boy's throwing film to Yessis, Yessis's first response was that the **sequence was off** and that was why the elbow broke; they then worked on running, cutting and throwing with special strength exercises and technical drills. The usable principle: **when a non-contact injury happens during the skill itself, analyse the skill's sequence, not only the volume.**

**When to apply** — Non-contact injuries that occur *during* a skill (a quarterback's elbow or shoulder, a receiver's hamstring in a route); building an individual plan where the exercise choice needs a reason; explaining to a sport coach why a particular lift is in a programme.

**When NOT to apply** — Qualitative sequence analysis is only as good as the analyst's eye and has no reliability data. The quarterback story is a single case told as a conversion experience — Yessis's diagnosis was accepted without any test, and the fracture had an obvious volume cause too. Moyer frames biomechanics as impractical, which undersells it: force plates, GPS and timing data are what confirm whether a qualitative diagnosis changed anything. Use qualitative analysis to generate the hypothesis and measurement to check it.

**Example** — A quarterback with medial elbow pain in fall camp: before only cutting his throw count, film him from the side and behind and check the order of hip rotation, trunk rotation and arm action; if the arm leads the trunk, that is a sequence target for the throwing coach and for trunk-rotation strength work.

**Related** — [[framework--sprint-coaching-eye-local-and-global-views]] — the sprint-specific application of this definition.

**When NOT to apply** — "Comparable video" needs to be genuinely comparable — same camera position, surface, footwear, effort and time of session — or the before-and-after mostly shows filming differences. A single pre and post time is within normal day-to-day variation for many athletes (hand-timed or single-trial gate times especially). Moyer's own examples do not separate his technical work from strength training, growth or simply being coached for six weeks, so they illustrate the reporting format, not proof that the method works. Also note he sells coaching and uses these clips to market it.

**Example** — Pre-camp and post-camp, each skill player runs two flying 10s through gates, filmed from the same spot at 10 yd. The report shows the best time each day next to paired stills at toe-off and touchdown — with a note if the conditions differed.

# A Low Reactivity Score May Be Foot Placement, Not a Stiffness Deficit

**What it is** — Moyer's caution about AI sprint software: a **low reactivity (stiffness) score** is often read as "this athlete is not stiff or bouncy enough", which points to plyometrics and stiffness work. He argues that for many of his athletes the real cause is **where the foot lands** — poor pawback / swing-leg retraction puts the foot too far in front, the athlete spends longer on the ground, and that long contact "presents itself as" low stiffness. The score is right that contact is long; it is wrong about why.

**Why it works** — Asserted: contact time and vertical movement, which such scores are likely built from, depend on both the spring qualities of the leg and on touchdown position. A foot that lands far ahead has to be passed over before push-off, lengthening contact even in a stiff leg. So the same number can have two causes that need different training. The mechanism is reasonable; the claim that it is the cause "with some of these athletes" is his observation.

**When to apply** — Any time a derived score (reactivity, stiffness, RSI from a sprint, contact-time flags from a wearable) drives a training decision. Before prescribing stiffness work, look at side-on film at touchdown: where is the foot relative to the hips? If it is far ahead, work retraction and contact position first and see whether the score moves.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **untested**: no data were shown for how often this happens, and the internal formula of the software he refers to (SpeedWorks' reactivity score) was not described. An athlete can have both problems. And the reverse error is possible — calling everything a foot-placement problem when the athlete genuinely sinks at contact.

**Example** — A receiver's reactivity score is the lowest in his group. Side film shows his foot landing well ahead of his hips with a fairly firm ankle and knee. Staff spend three weeks on pawback and wicket work instead of adding depth jumps, and the score rises with no change in jump testing.

**Related** — [[principle--pair-sprint-change-with-video-and-a-time]].

**What it is** — Three of Moyer's "results" cases from lesson 11, each shown as before/after video.
1. **High-school football player, ~6 weeks.** Diagnosis by eye: poor projection ("a spinner, Fred Flintstone kind of runner", tall and lanky) and poor stiffness ("mushes"). Work: lots of ankle- and calf-focused plyometrics, many single-leg calf raises, and heavy sled work. 3. **High-school sprinter.** Only calf work and swing-leg retraction work — "we didn't change much as far as heavy sleds or squatting". After, she lands attacking back and down instead of dropping straight down. No times given.

**Why it works** — Moyer's reading: fixing the specific key action he identified (projection and stiffness in case 1; retraction in case 3) produced the visible change. That is his interpretation.

**When to apply** — As worked examples of matching a diagnosis to a narrow training emphasis, and of the reporting format (video plus a time).

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **untested**. If so, the total gain is 0.10 s, not the "two tenths" he states. Single-trial times of this size are within normal variation for hand or single-gate timing, and the timing method was not given. Treat these as illustrations, not evidence.

**Example** — Case 3 is the cleanest template for Baylor use: one diagnosed action (retraction), one narrow training emphasis, and a visible, filmable change in touchdown position — the kind of case worth reproducing with gate times attached.

# Measuring a Long Swing Lever: 66.6° to 45° in a Pro Athlete

**What it is** — A professional athlete (context across lessons 6, 7 and the live sessions suggests an NFL player with a hamstring history, though the lessons do not confirm it is the same person) had a switching problem: the swing leg did not fold, creating a **long lever**, and he had a long history of soft-tissue treatment on his hip flexors. Moyer froze a side-on frame in **Dartfish** and measured the swing-leg angle at **66.6°**. After **one to two months** ("a month later, two months later") of **pails and rails** (FRC-style isometric range work), **Lila wearable resistance** and **wicket runs**, the same measure was **45°** on the stop frame — "we took off 21 degrees". He claims this is faster, more effective, and less wear on the hip flexors and rectus femoris.

**Why it works** — Asserted: a shorter lever is easier and faster to swing forward, so the thigh can come through without the hip flexors and rectus femoris having to drive a long, heavy pendulum. That follows from basic moment-of-inertia physics; that it improved his speed or reduced his injury risk was not measured.

**When to apply** — The useful part is the **method**: turn a by-eye fault into a number with a single frame from comparable side-on video. At Baylor this is a cheap way to track fold-up side to side in an athlete with a hamstring history, or across an RTP.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **untested**. Moyer did not define the angle (most likely the knee angle between thigh and shank at a point in swing — a smaller angle means more fold), nor which frame, nor camera set-up; a single frame at a slightly different moment of swing can change such an angle by many degrees. No speed data were reported. Three interventions ran together, and Moyer coaches with and markets wearable resistance (Lila), so the attribution to it is conflicted. Before using this measure yourself, fix the frame rule (e.g. the frame where the swing-leg thigh passes the stance leg), camera height and distance, and average across several strides and both legs.

**Example** — A cornerback returning from a left hamstring strain: at the frame where the swing thigh passes the stance leg, left knee angle 70°, right 52°. Re-measured every two weeks through RTP alongside NordBord asymmetry, it gives a running-specific number to go with the strength one.

**Related** — [[claim--long-swing-lever-and-heel-strike-hamstring-hypothesis]].

# Technique Analysis: The Sequence of Key Force-Producing Actions and the Muscles Doing Them

**What it is** — Moyer's (and his mentor Michael Yessis's) definition. **Biomechanics** is the physics of movement — numbers, forces, Newton's laws — and on its own "doesn't give us much in the way of practicality": a coach who knows an angle or a force still has to decide what to do. **Technique analysis** combines biomechanics with kinesiology into a **qualitative assessment of three things**: (1) the **key force-producing actions**, (2) the **sequence** in which they happen, and (3) **which muscles do them, where in the range, and how**. The muscle part is what makes it actionable — it names the exercise to train.

**Why it works** — Knowing the sequence and the working muscles lets the analyst go straight from "what is wrong" to "what to train", which a number alone does not do. Moyer's origin story makes the principle concrete: as a high-school strength coach in 2010, he saw his starting quarterback's elbow fracture while throwing a pass with no contact, after a summer of heavy throwing volume. When they sent the boy's throwing film to Yessis, Yessis's first response was that the **sequence was off** and that was why the elbow broke; they then worked on running, cutting and throwing with special strength exercises and technical drills. The usable principle: **when a non-contact injury happens during the skill itself, analyse the skill's sequence, not only the volume.**

**When to apply** — Non-contact injuries that occur *during* a skill (a quarterback's elbow or shoulder, a receiver's hamstring in a route); building an individual plan where the exercise choice needs a reason; explaining to a sport coach why a particular lift is in a programme.

**When NOT to apply** — Qualitative sequence analysis is only as good as the analyst's eye and has no reliability data. The quarterback story is a single case told as a conversion experience — Yessis's diagnosis was accepted without any test, and the fracture had an obvious volume cause too. Moyer frames biomechanics as impractical, which undersells it: force plates, GPS and timing data are what confirm whether a qualitative diagnosis changed anything. Use qualitative analysis to generate the hypothesis and measurement to check it.

**Example** — A quarterback with medial elbow pain in fall camp: before only cutting his throw count, film him from the side and behind and check the order of hip rotation, trunk rotation and arm action; if the arm leads the trunk, that is a sequence target for the throwing coach and for trunk-rotation strength work.

**Related** — [[framework--sprint-coaching-eye-local-and-global-views]] — the sprint-specific application of this definition.

# Measuring a Long Swing Lever: 66.6° to 45° in a Pro Athlete

**What it is** — A professional athlete (context across lessons 6, 7 and the live sessions suggests an NFL player with a hamstring history, though the lessons do not confirm it is the same person) had a switching problem: the swing leg did not fold, creating a **long lever**, and he had a long history of soft-tissue treatment on his hip flexors. Moyer froze a side-on frame in **Dartfish** and measured the swing-leg angle at **66.6°**. After **one to two months** ("a month later, two months later") of **pails and rails** (FRC-style isometric range work), **Lila wearable resistance** and **wicket runs**, the same measure was **45°** on the stop frame — "we took off 21 degrees". He claims this is faster, more effective, and less wear on the hip flexors and rectus femoris.

**Why it works** — Asserted: a shorter lever is easier and faster to swing forward, so the thigh can come through without the hip flexors and rectus femoris having to drive a long, heavy pendulum. That follows from basic moment-of-inertia physics; that it improved his speed or reduced his injury risk was not measured.

**When to apply** — The useful part is the **method**: turn a by-eye fault into a number with a single frame from comparable side-on video. At Baylor this is a cheap way to track fold-up side to side in an athlete with a hamstring history, or across an RTP.

**When NOT to apply** — Marked **untested**. Moyer did not define the angle (most likely the knee angle between thigh and shank at a point in swing — a smaller angle means more fold), nor which frame, nor camera set-up; a single frame at a slightly different moment of swing can change such an angle by many degrees. No speed data were reported. Three interventions ran together, and Moyer coaches with and markets wearable resistance (Lila), so the attribution to it is conflicted. Before using this measure yourself, fix the frame rule (e.g. the frame where the swing-leg thigh passes the stance leg), camera height and distance, and average across several strides and both legs.

**Example** — A cornerback returning from a left hamstring strain: at the frame where the swing thigh passes the stance leg, left knee angle 70°, right 52°. Re-measured every two weeks through RTP alongside NordBord asymmetry, it gives a running-specific number to go with the strength one.

**Related** — [[claim--long-swing-lever-and-heel-strike-hamstring-hypothesis]].

# In Return to Run, Watch Them Run

**What it is** — Moyer's complaint from years in an orthopaedic practice: rehab clinics treat a running injury (patellar pain, a hamstring strain) with generic exercises — TKEs, knee extensions, Nordics, bridges, isometrics, then a short-to-long running programme — **without ever watching the athlete run**. The pain goes, the athlete "goes back to running like crap", and the injury returns. His process instead: (1) gather **injury history, training background and current goals**; (2) know the **sport's demands**; (3) **watch and film them run** before choosing interventions; (4) **re-film after** the rehab block to see whether mechanics or left-right differences actually changed. He states that "gym strength is less important than how they apply force to the ground during running", so a running-specific test is essential for judging progress.

**Why it works** — Clinical tests and gym strength measure capacities; sprinting is the task that injures. If the running pattern that loaded the tissue is unchanged, capacity gains may not protect it. Filming before and after gives a direct check that the task has changed, not just the tests. The logic is sound; his framing that "research indicates biomechanical analysis can predict injuries" overstates the evidence, which is mostly associations.

**When to apply** — Every lower-limb soft-tissue RTP at Baylor: film the athlete's running at each progression stage (tempo, 75%, 90%, max), side and front, and compare with pre-injury film when it exists. Pair film with GPS max velocity and force-plate or NordBord asymmetry so the decision has both a task view and a capacity view. Moyer quotes that about a third of hamstring injuries recur, with the highest risk in the first two weeks back — the window where running film is most useful.

**When NOT to apply** — Film shows *how* they run, not tissue readiness; it does not replace strength, range, imaging or clinical criteria, and "runs well" is not a clearance test. Changing mechanics during late rehab also adds a new stressor at a vulnerable time — record mechanics, but be careful about making big technique changes in the final days before clearance. His injury statistics (25–35% of team-sport injuries are hamstrings, "some show 50%") were quoted loosely.

**Example** — A cornerback cleared on NordBord symmetry and pain-free isometrics is filmed at 90%. Side view shows his injured leg still swinging a long lever and landing further ahead than the other. Staff hold the progression one stage and add swing-leg work before max-velocity exposure.

**Related** — [[claim--long-swing-lever-and-heel-strike-hamstring-hypothesis]]; [[principle--action-capacity-is-not-skill]] — agreement: capacity scores do not show how the task is performed.

# The Sprint Coaching Eye: Local Actions and Global Views

**What it is** — Moyer's two-level way of watching a sprinter. The **local view** is three "key force-producing actions": (1) **knee drive** — the thigh driven forward from behind the body right after toe-off; (2) **pawback** (swing-leg retraction) — the leg driven back and down into the ground; (3) **ankle joint extension** — plantar flexion through push-off. The **global view** is three qualities built out of those actions: (a) **projection** — how far the pelvis / centre of mass travels from toe-off to the next foot contact (also read from thigh spread in the air); (b) **switching** — how well the limbs exchange, i.e. knee drive and pawback happening together (what Clark calls thigh angular velocity or "whip from the hip"); (c) **stiffness** — how well the body *withstands* the landing at the hip, knee and ankle rather than sinking. His working order: **watch globally live, then film and break the global fault down into its local actions.** The global qualities are the symptom; the local actions are where the training goes.

**Why it works** — The split borrows Verkhoshansky's idea (itself a rename of Bernstein's essential vs. non-essential variables) that a skill has a few **key movements** that set its power output and **secondary movements** that assist them. If you improve the key movements and how they link, the whole action improves. Applied to observation, that becomes a filter: do not chase every visible difference between this athlete and a model sprinter; ask whether the three key actions are doing their job. The link from knee drive to pawback is asserted as reciprocal — a higher thigh in front gives a longer, faster path back to the ground — and is consistent with Clark's thigh-angular-velocity work (see [[claim--thigh-angular-velocity-and-sprint-speed]]). The claim that exactly these three actions are *the* key movements of sprinting is Moyer's (and Yessis's) selection, not a validated taxonomy.

**When to apply** — First look at a new athlete; speed-group sorting in the first weeks of camp; a return-to-run progression where you need a shared vocabulary between athletic performance and athletic medicine staff. The global words (projection, switching, stiffness) are quick enough to use live on a field; the local words are for slow-motion film.

**When NOT to apply** — This is one coach's observation scheme, **not a validated screen**: no inter-rater reliability, no cut-offs, and "good projection" or "poor stiffness" are judgements by eye. The global terms also overlap with commercial scoring (SpeedWorks "projection, switching, reactivity"), so a number on a report is not an independent check on your eye. It covers linear sprinting only — it says nothing about cutting, backpedal or pursuit angles, which is most of a football player's high-speed work. And the Bernstein/Verkhoshansky lineage does not settle which movements are "key"; the ecological view in the Myszka material argues that athletes solve the same problem with different movements, so a non-standard action is not automatically a fault.

**Example** — A 230-lb tight end looks "short and choppy" live (global: poor projection, frequent switching). On side-view film the thighs barely separate at toe-off and he stands upright within five yards (local: weak knee drive, little push through the ankle). The training target becomes the knee drive and ankle push, not "take longer strides".

**Related** — [[principle--degeneracy-precedes-dexterity]] — tension: key-movement thinking assumes a correct core pattern; degeneracy says many patterns can be correct. [[heuristic--how-to-watch-film]] — agreement on watching live for the gestalt and on film for detail.

# Match the Sprint Fault to a Range-of-Motion Check Before Choosing the Fix

**What it is** — Moyer does not go straight from a film fault to a drill. He first asks whether the athlete *can* reach the position, by checking passive and then active range at the joints that feed that fault. His mapping (lesson 6, with the tests shown in live session 3):
- **Poor projection / stands up early** → hip extension (he likes the Thomas test), ankle dorsiflexion, ankle plantar flexion, big-toe extension. Example: a soccer player who could barely lift his toes onto a yoga block ran exactly like that.
- **Long lever / poor fold-up** → active knee flexion in prone: can the athlete lift the heel toward the buttock with the hamstrings? He accepts a gap of about a pinky-to-thumb span; more than that needs work. He says this check is missing from the hamstring literature.
- **Straight knee at toe-off / poor ankle extension** → calf strength and ankle range (his reading; disputed).
- **Rotation at toe-off, not reaching the big toe** → hip, ankle or foot — check all three.
- **Dorsiflexion** → knee-to-wall, heel staying heavy and knee tracking over the **third** toe (not collapsing inward); he uses about 4 in from the wall as "adequate" and cites 20° as the usual target.

**Why it works** — A fault can come from a capacity limit (range, strength) or from coordination. A cue or drill cannot fix a range limit, and range work will not fix a timing problem. Checking first keeps the intervention matched to the cause.

**When to apply** — After the film review and before writing the individual block; in RTP, where the medical staff already record range, share the numbers rather than re-testing.

**When NOT to apply** — The mapping is Moyer's reasoning, **not a validated diagnostic chain**: normal range does not rule out a range contribution at sprint speed, and a range deficit does not prove it causes the fault. His thresholds are rough (a hand-span, "about 4 inches") and he admits they are not scientific. Treat a limited joint as a hypothesis to test by re-filming after the range improves.

**Example** — A defensive end shows little thigh spread and rises by 5 yd. His Thomas test shows a hip flexor limit and his knee-to-wall is 2 in. Staff add loaded hip-extension and ankle range work for three weeks before adding any projection drills, then re-film.

**Related** — [[framework--sprint-fault-observation-checklist]] — the faults this check follows.

## 2. Review digest

**Exact figures stated**

*Lesson 5 (repeated in Live 2):*
- Soleus and gastrocnemius give 77% of vertical and 60% of horizontal centre-of-mass acceleration.
- The Achilles "accumulates 75–90%" of mechanical energy. No source is given.
- The foot-ankle returns 60–70% of landing energy.
- From a 1981 *Soviet Sports Review* article from Zatsiorsky's lab: takeoff external energy +340 J; knee muscles 31 J; plantar flexors 192 J ("more than six times").
- Push-off gives "up to 20%" of sprint force. In Live 2 Moyer says he doesn't know where Yessis got this.
- Knee extension from 164° to 168° is "useless"; the knee should not exceed 165° at the end of takeoff.

*Lesson 7:*
- Hamstrings are 25–30% of team-sport injuries (he later says 25–35%, and "you can find 50%").
- One third recur, with the highest risk in the first two weeks back.

*Lesson 11:*
- College WR 10-yd split 1.25 → 1.15 s, and 1.73 → 1.63 s.
- Pro athlete swing angle 66.6° → 45° in "a month… two months".
- High-school football case: about 6 weeks, no times given.

*Live 3 results, badly garbled in the transcript:*
- One athlete: "one five two" → "one one five", unreadable.
- A football player: 10-yd 1.82 → 1.62, and max speed "6.994 → 7.64 m/s".
- Knee-to-wall of about 4 in; 20° dorsiflexion "usually" cited; 30–35° for a soleus test; a pinky-to-thumb span as the acceptable heel-to-butt gap.

**Citations named**
- Bernstein; Verkhoshansky (key and secondary movements); Zatsiorsky (*Science and Practice of Strength Training* diagram).
- *Soviet Sports Review* 1981 (takeoff biomechanics) and 1989 (fatigue-induced technique change: hip-flexor fatigue leads to lower thigh height, less pawback, longer support).
- Ken Clark: "whip from the hip" (thigh angular velocity), horizontal foot speed, "negative foot speed" with shoe-mounted inertial sensors, and the two-mass model with Weyand.
- A Peter Weyand quote. The "stiff angle/ankle" wording differs between lessons 5 and 14.
- Heiderscheit (hamstring injury in late swing).
- JB Morin (transcribed "Marin"): horizontal force and hamstring injury.
- J. J. Wild, via Jonas Dodoo / Speedworks. Plus quotes from Randy Huntington and Stu McMillan; Yessis throughout.

**Wild's four profiles as Moyer gives them**

| Profile | Description | Moyer's training response | Injury sites Moyer attributes to Wild |
|---|---|---|---|
| Q1 Bounders | Step length, air-based; hips rise too early, low braking | Make more ground-based. Live 3: ankle pails and rails, heavy sleds, single-leg calf raises, pawback work (banded marches, then banded bounding) | Calf, Achilles, foot |
| Q2 Drivers | Step length, ground-based; hips low, no rise, "mushy" | Make bouncier. Live 3: foot isometrics, "delay squats" (probably pause squats; unclear), pawbacks, extensive jumps for stiffness | Patella and quad; hip and thigh |
| Q3 Spinners | Frequency, ground-based; "spin the wheels" | Better projection plus more bounce (outline only) | Hip flexors, adductors |
| Q4 Bouncers | Frequency, air-based; "Fred Flintstone" | Better projection and more force (outline only) | Calf, Achilles, foot, hip flexors (the most injury types) |

His goal is to move everyone "toward the middle"; no quadrant is better than another. In practice he uses 4–5 bucket exercises in the first 10–15 minutes of a team session, with the rest common.

**Claims that need checking or look wrong**
- **The WR times don't add up.** A "second 10" of 1.73 s slower than the first 10 is implausible, so 1.73 is probably the 20-yd time. In that case the gain is 0.10 s, not the "two tenths" he states.
- **"Fred Flintstone" is used for different profiles.** In lesson 7 it means bouncers (Q4). In lesson 11 he calls the high-school football player "a spinner, Fred Flintstone kind of runner". In lesson 6 it means little thigh spread.
- **"Never assessed a non-contact injury in a non-heel-striker"** has obvious selection bias, and he treats heel strike and overstride as one thing.
- **"Research indicates biomechanical analysis can predict injuries"** overstates what is mostly association research.
- **The 77%/60% figure** looks like a musculoskeletal-simulation output. I noted in the entry that hip work generally dominates at top speed; the entry says this is hedged and should be verified.
- **The Wild material needs checking:** the injury-site data, whether the four labels are Wild's or Speedworks'/Moyer's, and Wild's full name.
- **He dismisses Clark as "regurgitating" the Soviets.** That is opinion.
- **The long-lever/hamstring link** is admitted chicken-or-egg.

**Products and commercial mentions**
- Software: ViewMotion, "Binary" (as transcribed), Altus, Ken Clark's app, SpeedWorks PSR (projection/switching/reactivity), Dartfish.
- Lila wearable resistance. Moyer coaches with and markets it, which is a conflict of interest in the 66°→45° case.
- FRS/FRC-style "pails and rails".
- Hawkins force plates (mentioned by a participant); New Balance shoes; Alex Natera isometrics.

**Which lessons are worth rewatching**
- **L6 (Assess): yes.** It has the most usable film examples.
- **L7: yes,** for the Wild section at 12:00–18:30.
- **L5:** the Live 2 section at 43:00–60:00 repeats it almost word for word, with a useful Q&A on "can't whip if the thigh doesn't go high" and casting.
- **L11:** only for the narration, which ends at 6:57; the rest is silent clips.
- **L12:** skip. It is a 4-minute origin story.
- **Live 3 at 1:35–1:43** (film review: ankle collapse, rotation, crossover) is good practice material.

**Best ideas for a college-football performance/rehab director**
1. **Film the run at each RTP stage** (side and front) and put it next to NordBord and GPS. Capacity scores don't show how the athlete performs the task.
2. **Use the global-then-local split.** Watch projection, switching and stiffness live; on film, trace each fault to knee drive, pawback or ankle extension.
3. **Turn the long-lever fault into a number** with a single-frame knee angle, compared left and right, for athletes with a hamstring history. You have to define the frame rule yourself; Moyer didn't.
4. **Before prescribing stiffness work from a low reactivity score, check where the foot lands.**
5. **Use Wild-style buckets** as a cheap way to individualise team speed sessions.

## 3. Moyer's observation checklist (compact)

**Contact first:** which part of the foot lands, and where relative to the hips and the knee. Heel strike ahead of the knee is his biggest flag.
- At contact, the space between the knees should be about zero; a gap means poor switching.

**Side view, upright:**
- A slight knee bend at toe-off. A straight knee he reads as an ankle/calf issue; this is disputed.
- Heel folds close to the buttock. A long lever means poor knee drive.
- Excessive heel recovery behind the body (the foot hides the buttocks from behind) means backside dominance.
- The thigh should rise in front, with the foot coming back and down, not straight down.
- How much the hip, knee and ankle sink at contact ("mush"); a bouncing ponytail shows vertical oscillation.

**Early acceleration:**
- Landing slightly ahead of the hips is fine; far ahead ("power walking") with a vertical shin at contact is a fault.
- Thigh spread at toe-off (projection).
- Standing upright by about 5 yd means poor projection.

**Front/rear (read from the ground up):**
- Rolls to and pushes through the big toe with a straight foot. Some rotation is fine; the degree matters.
- Ankle collapse; external rotation at toe-off.
- Pelvic drop or side-to-side "sloshing".
- Crossover gait.
- The swing-leg foot should be hidden behind the thigh from the front.

**Then:**
- Film several sprints from several angles and note surface, shoes and whether the rep was timed.
- Check ROM, matched to the fault:
  - Projection: hip extension (Thomas test), dorsiflexion (knee-to-wall over the third toe), plantar flexion, big toe.
  - Long lever: prone active heel-to-butt.
  - Rotation: hip, ankle and foot.

## 3. Moyer's observation checklist (compact)

**Contact first:** which part of the foot lands, and where relative to the hips and the knee. Heel strike ahead of the knee is his biggest flag.
- At contact, the space between the knees should be about zero; a gap means poor switching.

**Side view, upright:**
- A slight knee bend at toe-off. A straight knee he reads as an ankle/calf issue; this is disputed.
- Heel folds close to the buttock. A long lever means poor knee drive.
- Excessive heel recovery behind the body (the foot hides the buttocks from behind) means backside dominance.
- The thigh should rise in front, with the foot coming back and down, not straight down.
- How much the hip, knee and ankle sink at contact ("mush"); a bouncing ponytail shows vertical oscillation.

**Early acceleration:**
- Landing slightly ahead of the hips is fine; far ahead ("power walking") with a vertical shin at contact is a fault.
- Thigh spread at toe-off (projection).
- Standing upright by about 5 yd means poor projection.

**Front/rear (read from the ground up):**
- Rolls to and pushes through the big toe with a straight foot. Some rotation is fine; the degree matters.
- Ankle collapse; external rotation at toe-off.
- Pelvic drop or side-to-side "sloshing".
- Crossover gait.
- The swing-leg foot should be hidden behind the thigh from the front.

**Then:**
- Film several sprints from several angles and note surface, shoes and whether the rep was timed.
- Check ROM, matched to the fault:
  - Projection: hip extension (Thomas test), dorsiflexion (knee-to-wall over the third toe), plantar flexion, big toe.
  - Long lever: prone active heel-to-butt.
  - Rotation: hip, ankle and foot.

**Best ideas for Eric:**
- Film athletes running at every return-to-play stage and put the film next to NordBord and GPS data.
- Track a single-frame knee-fold angle, left against right, for players with a hamstring history.
- Check where the foot lands before treating a low software stiffness score as a stiffness problem.
